query: For phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys, what single intervention could improve glass-forming ability and the thermal stability of the amorphous state? Formulate one testable hypothesis that specifies the intervention without presupposing its class, the mechanism by which it would act, the predicted improvement relative to an otherwise comparable baseline, the conditions under which it should or should not work, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A staged sub-Tg annealing process applied immediately after melt-spinning improves both the glass-forming ability and the thermal stability of phosphorus-containing high-entropy amorphous alloys by relaxing internal stresses and promoting beneficial short-range ordering that impedes crystallization.
generation.material_initial_state: Phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloy in an amorphous state produced via rapid quenching/melt-spinning.
generation.intervention: Apply a single thermal/thermomechanical treatment by holding the amorphous sample at approximately 0.8 of its glass transition temperature (Tg) for 60–120 seconds immediately after production.
generation.conditions: This intervention is expected to be effective when performed immediately post-quenching under an atmosphere that prevents oxidation, ensuring the temperature remains below Tg to allow stress relaxation without initiating crystallization. Its benefits may be limited if the treatment temperature or duration exceed thresholds that trigger devitrification.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced short-range atomic ordering and reduced free volume resulting from the relaxation of internal stresses during the sub-Tg anneal.
generation.mechanism: The sub-Tg annealing treatment allows slight atomic rearrangements that relax residual stresses while preserving the overall disordered structure. This promotes a favorable short-range order that increases the energy barrier for crystallization, thereby stabilizing the amorphous phase and indirectly improving glass formation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to non-annealed samples, the treated alloys will exhibit an increased glass-forming ability and a higher onset temperature for exothermic crystallization (as seen by differential scanning calorimetry) due to the improved stability of the amorphous state.
generation.baseline: Phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys produced by melt-spinning without any subsequent sub-Tg thermal treatment.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected only when the annealing is maintained at ~0.8Tg and within a 60–120 s window. Exceeding this temperature or time may induce crystallization, while insufficient annealing may not adequately relieve internal stresses.
generation.uncertainty: The exact optimal temperature and time window may vary with composition, and quantitative improvements in the onset crystallization temperature are to be determined. Further optimization is necessary to fine-tune these parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy samples via melt-spinning. Subject one set to the sub-Tg annealing treatment (maintaining ~0.8Tg for 60–120 seconds) and keep the other set as a control without any annealing. Characterize both sets using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to identify the onset of crystallization, and use X-ray diffraction (XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to assess changes in short-range ordering and internal stresses.
measurements: Changes in the diffuse peak positions and widths in XRD patterns
Microstructural changes indicating short-range ordering from TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not show a statistically significant increase in the onset crystallization temperature or improved indicators of short-range ordering relative to the control group, the hypothesis is considered falsified.

This study focuses on the high-entropy alloy Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20, selected for its anticipated amorphization potential resulting from high configurational entropy and phosphorus addition. The cooling rates were systematically varied, with slow cooling averaging approximately 52 K/s, accelerated cooling at 3018 K/s, and melt-spinning achieving rapid cooling rates in the range of 10⁵–10⁶ K/s. We investigated the alloy’s phase transformations and microstructural evolution under different cooling conditions, including slow cooling on a copper plate, accelerated cooling after remelting, and rapid quenching using melt-spinning. By characterizing the resulting structures using XRD, SEM, TEM, and Mössbauer spectroscopy, we aim to advance the understanding of processing-condition effects on phase stability and amorphization in phosphorus-enriched HEAs, providing insights for the development of HEAs with tailored properties. The intensity profile of the diffraction rings observed in TEM, with two broad peaks at wave vector values of k = 1.169 nm−1 and k = 2.002 nm−1, corresponds to characteristic features of reciprocal space scattering in amorphous structures. These values are indicative of the short-range atomic ordering typical of metallic glasses based on transition metals and phosphorus. The diffuse peaks in this study are consistent with XRD results, which revealed a broad intensity maximum characteristic of amorphous structures. cited_evidence.text: As shown in the differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) measurement in Figure 4D, the crystallization of the amorphous particles is an exothermic process and begins at approximately 375 °C, which is exactly the same temperature where the rapid decrease of the FWHM in Figure 4C starts, and the required thermal energy kBT is achieved to overcome the activation energy. Note that for the determination of the plot in Figure 4C, more temperature steps were considered than those shown in Figure 4B. However, for clarity reasons, the full data set of 94 SAED patterns is not shown and can be found in the Supporting Information File 2 as a video file. The observation of amorphous particles transforming into a crystalline phase validates that the amorphous phase is metastable and forms under kinetic control, whereas the crystalline structure is the thermodynamically favored one [], and thermodynamic control is dominant when activation energy barriers are overcome by heating.

decision.trend: Early studies on high-entropy metallic glasses (e.g., NbNiZrTiCo) showed that a high degree of disorder can trigger unusual glass-to-glass transitions and affect thermal stability. Subsequently, direct work on phosphorus-containing compositions (Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20) revealed that combining P with multicomponent alloys significantly enhances glass-forming ability (GFA) and shifts phase transformation temperatures to lower values, indicating strong compositional effects and the influence of cooling rate. However, the conditions under which glass-forming kinetics and subsequent thermal stability can be jointly optimized remain insufficiently explored, beyond demonstrating that both intensive rapid quenching and compositional complexity help achieve amorphization.
decision.unsolved: Although rapid cooling and compositional complexity both favor glass formation, there is still no clear single-step process proven to simultaneously improve GFA and retain an amorphous state upon heating. In particular, achieving robust, stable amorphous phases under varied service temperatures is challenging, and it remains unclear how best to tweak processing conditions—independently of new elemental additions—to suppress crystallization kinetics after initial vitrification.
decision.lever: Implement a staged sub-Tg annealing process (e.g., ~0.8Tg for 60–120 s) immediately after melt-spinning and before any full crystallization can initiate, to relax internal stresses and promote favored short-range ordering without triggering devitrification
decision.why: Recent evidence shows that subtle thermal treatments can stabilize high-entropy amorphous structures by promoting short-range order while preserving overall disorder. For phosphorus-bearing high-entropy alloys, a short, carefully controlled sub-Tg anneal can minimize internal free volume and reduce the driving force for subsequent crystallization, thus improving both GFA and thermal stability in the final amorphous structure, without introducing additional elements. This approach builds on the success of rapid quenching from the melt (as evidenced by the Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 study) yet addresses the open challenge of preserving the amorphous state at higher temperatures.
